title: $11,195 through Donors Choose - A Reflection on Generosity
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart reflects on eleven thousand dollars of classroom resources funded by strangers through Donors Choose and extracts seven lessons from a decade of requests. He begins with failure, analyzing why his first project as a second-year teacher in Baltimore went unfunded: overpriced vendors, a smaller donor pool and inexperience. The central practical finding is that he is a poor predictor of which projects will matter most, illustrated by an iPad that never integrated with school systems against a small book request from a student named Kyle that produced worn, well-read copies. From that he derives the strategy of many small responsible requests rather than a few large ones, noting that hundred to two hundred dollar projects rarely fail while thousand dollar ones often do. He also describes batching, writing several proposals in one sitting with shared copy, which covers a quarter of requests in about an hour since projects stay live for ninety days. Two softer lessons close the piece: donors need to see the impact of their giving, and funding notifications function as evidence for a teacher that strangers believe the work matters. The piece carries repeated plugs for the author's paid starter kit, but the operational advice stands on its own.
points: Stuart's key correction is that teachers are poor predictors of impact, so the sensible strategy is many small requests rather than betting on one large project.
Hundred to two hundred dollar requests almost always fund while thousand dollar requests frequently fail, which argues for chunking a large vision into small proposals.

Responsible asking means requesting only what your professional judgment says will promote students' long-term flourishing, and thinking through what could go wrong, which is far more with technology than with books.
Batch-writing several proposals in one sitting, reusing copy across similar projects, covers most of a quarter's fundraising in about an hour.
Transparency about impact is what sustains giving, which is why he treats the thank-you process as part of the work rather than an afterthought.
quotes: During this past school year, a group of mostly strangers donated $4,197 worth of books to my classroom library ( here's the list ). I didn't earn a grant for this; I have no wealthy benefactors; and I didn't ask for donations from readers of this blog or its social networks.

Donors Choose has been around for twice as long now as it had been when I wrote my first project. People like Oprah and Stephen Colbert have promoted it since then. This means there are waaay more folks who are surfing Donors Choose looking to give to great classrooms.

The opportunities donors have given my kids really can't be quantified. Again and again, I've seen kids' minds light on fire — for some through whole-class readings of All Quiet on the Western Front or Things Fall Apart ; for others, through independent reading books from our classroom library; still for others, through some of the sweet tech Donors Choose has given us, like a podcast recorder or an iPad.

Unfortunately, technology is tricky. What I thought would be an easy marriage between the iPad and our school's existing technology was… well, not such an easy marriage. The iPad did serve some purposes in my room, but none as grand as I had hoped.

When I say responsibly, I mean only ask for stuff that you, in your professional judgment, believe will promote the long-term flourishing of your kids. Try to think through what could go wrong — not much can go wrong with books; plenty can go wrong with technology.

But with that said, if you've got a sweet vision for classroom resources that your kids need, it is smart to have a few lures in the water at all times. If your vision is huge, break it down into $100-$200 projects.

I don't know about you, but I can often get derailed by a single negative comment from a student, parent, or colleague. Yet every time I get one of those magical emails from Donors Choose saying, “Congratulations, your project is fully funded,” it's proof that, indeed, I am not alone in this.
